title: ALMA beneath the stars
caption: ALMA antennas beneath the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: Several dish antennas point up at targets in the night sky, while the Milky Way slices through the frame, surrounded by a sea of stars. These are 12-metre antennas, part of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, known as ALMA.

ALMA does not take pictures in visible light the way the camera that made this photograph does. Its antennas collect light at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, which lie far beyond the range our eyes can detect. Many antennas working together can act like one much larger telescope.

The Milky Way overhead is our galaxy seen from inside, a band formed by the combined glow of countless faraway stars, interrupted by clouds of dust. It is the sort of cold dust and gas in galaxies like ours that instruments such as ALMA are designed to study. The antennas, meanwhile, are turned toward targets of their own somewhere in that sky.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at ALMA. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure collects much more light than the eye, so the Milky Way appears brighter and more detailed than it would in person.

explore: ALMA is located on the Chajnantor plateau, high in the Chilean Atacama Desert. Its 12-metre antennas are shown here turned toward the night sky, each one a single part of the much larger array that works together as one instrument.
alt: Several dish antennas pointing at the night sky, with the Milky Way cutting across a field of stars.
